title: Tracking setup lab: pixel, Conversions API and postbacks
summary: A hands-on lab where you build, alone and click by click, the tracking that the Tracking basics module explained: a pixel with events, Conversions API with deduplication, affiliate postbacks forwarded to Meta and Telegram join tracking. You finish with a tested end-to-end setup and a troubleshooting table, so you never spend on data you have not checked.

lessons.title: Your tracking plan on one page
objectives: By the end you can draw your whole tracking system on one page: ad, lander, offer, network, server and Meta

steps.p: This module is a lab. By the end you will have a working pixel, Conversions API events, network postbacks and Telegram join tracking, set up by you alone. It starts with a plan on one page, because most broken tracking was never planned. Ten minutes on paper saves days of confused numbers.
steps.more: Module 5 (Tracking basics) taught what pixels, the Conversions API, click IDs and postbacks are. Here you set each one up, step by step, in the order they depend on each other. Keep a notebook or a sheet open. At the end of every lesson you will have one more piece working, and you will test it before moving on.

d.s: Module 5 explained the ideas. This module builds them.

steps.say: Welcome to the lab. In this module you'll actually build your tracking, by yourself. By the end you'll have a working pixel, Conversions API events, network postbacks and Telegram join tracking. Module five explained the ideas. Here, you set each piece up in the order they depend on each other. So keep a notebook or a sheet open. And we start with a plan on one page, because ten minutes on paper saves days of confused numbers.

steps.p: Money is lost quietly when tracking is missing. Meta can only learn from events it receives. If your deposits are counted by the network but never sent to Meta, the algorithm keeps finding people who click, not people who deposit. You pay for that confusion every day.
steps.more: Example: a buyer spends $40 a day for 3 days, $120 in total. The network panel shows 4 FTDs at a $40 payout, so $160 revenue. Meta shows zero purchases because no postback was connected. The buyer looks at Ads Manager, sees no results and kills a campaign that was actually profitable. The same mistake in reverse also happens: a double-firing pixel shows twice the leads and the buyer scales something that loses money.

d.label: spent before anyone noticed the postback was never set up

steps.say: Here's why this matters. Meta can only learn from the events it receives. Look at the number on screen: one hundred and twenty dollars. In this example, a buyer spends forty dollars a day for three days. The network counts four F T Ds, first time deposits, at a forty dollar payout, so one hundred and sixty dollars in revenue. But Meta sees zero, because no postback was connected. The buyer kills a campaign that was actually profitable. And the reverse happens too: a double-firing pixel shows twice the leads, and the buyer scales a loser.

steps.h: The whole system on one page
steps.p: This is the setup you will build. The visitor sees your ad and lands on your page. The pixel reports what happens on your page. Your offer link carries a click ID to the network. When the person registers or deposits, the network calls your server with a postback, and your server tells Meta through the Conversions API.
steps.say: This map is the setup you'll build. Follow it from the left. The visitor sees your Meta ad and clicks through to your lander. The pixel on your lander reports PageView and Lead to Meta. Your offer link carries a click I D, in sub one, to the offer site. When the person signs up or deposits, the network calls your server with a postback. And your server tells Meta through the Conversions API. Every lesson in this module builds one piece of this picture.

steps.h: Pages you control and pages you do not
steps.p: This is the key fact for affiliates. You can put the pixel on your own lander. You usually cannot put it on the offer site, because the advertiser owns it. So events on your page come from the pixel, and events on the offer site come back to you as postbacks.
steps.more: Some networks let you place a pixel on the offer's thank-you page. Many trading and iGaming advertisers do not allow it, and even when they do, the deposit often happens days later on another device. A server-to-server postback is the reliable path for money events. That is why lesson 5 is all about postbacks.

steps.h: The four parts you will build
steps.p: Every setup in this module is built from four parts. You will add them in this order, and each one depends on the one before it. Do not skip ahead: a postback is useless if your click ID was never passed to the offer.
d: Pixel|Code on your pages that reports browser events (lesson 2 and 3)
Conversions API|Your server sends events straight to Meta (lesson 4)
Click ID and sub IDs|One ID that follows each click to the network (lesson 5)
Postback|The network calls your server when money happens (lesson 5)
steps.say: Every setup here is built from these four parts, and you'll add them in this order. First, the pixel, code on your pages that reports browser events. Second, the Conversions API, where your server sends events straight to Meta. Third, the click I D and sub I Ds, one I D that follows each click to the network. And fourth, the postback, where the network calls your server when money happens. Don't skip ahead. A postback is useless if your click I D was never passed to the offer.

steps.h: Can your budget feed the event?
steps.p: Meta learns faster when an ad set gets enough of the event it optimises for. Before choosing Purchase as your goal, check how many you can afford per day. Deeper events are worth more but arrive less often.
steps.more: Meta has said in its help pages that an ad set needs roughly 50 optimisation events in a week to leave the learning phase. We are not certain this number is current; check Meta's Help Center. Treat it as a direction, not a rule: the point is that 8 events a week is very little signal, and 140 is plenty.

steps.h: Worked example: choosing the starting event
steps.p: Example: $40 a day. Lead costs about $2, registration $8, FTD $35. Leads: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 a day, 140 a week. Registrations: 40 ÷ 8 = 5 a day, 35 a week. FTDs: 40 ÷ 35 ≈ 1.1 a day, about 8 a week. Start on Lead or registration, send FTDs anyway, and move deeper as volume grows.
steps.more: Sending FTDs to Meta even when you do not optimise for them still helps: you can see them in reporting, and you can switch the optimisation event later without rebuilding anything. The costs here are illustrative; yours depend on geo, offer and creative.

d.text: $40/day: Lead ≈ 140/week, Registration ≈ 35/week, FTD ≈ 8/week. Starting rule to adapt: optimise for the deepest event you can get at least 35 to 50 times a week.

steps.h: Compliance: plan privacy from day one
steps.p: Tracking uses personal data. Your lander needs a clear privacy notice that says you use the Meta pixel and share data with ad partners. Where the law requires consent before tracking, ask first.
steps.more: This is not legal advice. Laws and their guidance change, and some countries require registration with a data protection authority once you process data at scale. Read the regulator's own page for each geo you run, and when money is involved, ask a qualified local lawyer.

steps.h: One pixel, installed once, on every page
steps.p: Why it matters: the base code is the foundation every other event sits on. If it is missing on one page, events from that page vanish. If it is installed twice, every event counts double and you scale on fake numbers. Get this right once and every later lesson works.

d.b: Install once. Verify. Then build on it.
d.s: Missing pixels lose data. Double pixels invent it.

steps.say: Here's why the base code matters so much. It's the foundation every other event sits on. If it's missing on one page, events from that page simply vanish. If it's installed twice, every event counts double, and you'd scale on fake numbers. The line on screen says it all: missing pixels lose data, double pixels invent it. So install once, verify, then build on it.

steps.p: Pick one route per website and stick to it. Mixing routes is the most common cause of double counting. If your site builder has a pixel field, use it. If you use Google Tag Manager already, use that. Otherwise paste the code by hand.

Google Tag Manager|Add the code as a tag that fires on all pages

steps.h: Worked example: clicks, page views, PageViews
steps.p: Example from day one. Ads Manager shows 1,000 link clicks and 720 landing page views. Events Manager shows 700 PageViews. 720 ÷ 1,000 = 72% of clickers waited for the page to load. PageView and landing page views are close, so the pixel is fine; the page is slow.
steps.more: Rough guide, varies by geo and network: on mobile data in many African markets, losing 20 to 35% between click and page view is common for slow pages. If PageView is far BELOW landing page views, check the pixel. If PageView is far ABOVE, look for double installation or a pixel firing on other sites. Starting rule to adapt: if landing page views are under 70% of link clicks, fix page speed before testing new ads.

steps.h: Worked example: value turns into ROAS
steps.p: Example: you spend $160. The network reports 5 FTDs at $40 each, sent to Meta as Purchase with value 40 and currency USD. Total value: 5 × 40 = $200. Meta shows ROAS of 200 ÷ 160 = 1.25. Without value, Meta could only count purchases, not money.
steps.more: Meta's ROAS is a guide, not your profit. The network is where you get paid, and it may reject some FTDs later. Profit = network revenue − spend = $200 − $160 = $40 in this example, if no FTDs are rejected. Value-based optimisation options exist in Meta for some objectives; they need steady value data first. steps.p: The browser and your server each send Lead with the same event_id. Meta sees two messages with the same event name and ID and keeps one. If either one is missing, the other still counts. That is the whole point of sending both.
steps.more: At the time of writing, Meta's documentation says browser and server events are deduplicated when event_name and event_id match and they arrive within about 48 hours of each other. Server events sent alone, such as postback deposits, do not need a browser twin, but still give them an event_id so retries do not double count.

steps.p: Example: over one day the pixel sends 60 Leads and your server sends 75. Both share the same event ID for 55 of them. Meta counts 60 + 75 − 55 = 80 unique leads. Without event IDs it would show 135, and your cost per lead would look 41% cheaper than it really is.
steps.more: Check: $160 ÷ 80 = $2.00. $160 ÷ 135 ≈ $1.19. ($2.00 − $1.19) ÷ $2.00 ≈ 41%. If you scaled on $1.19 against a $1.60 break-even, you would be losing money while the dashboard said you were winning. Starting rule to adapt: if a new server setup makes results jump by more than 30% overnight, check deduplication before you add budget.

steps.h: The money happens where you cannot see it
steps.p: Why it matters: registrations and deposits happen on the advertiser's site. The only way you, and Meta, learn about them is the network's postback. Without it, Meta optimises on clicks and leads while your profit is decided somewhere it cannot see.

d.b: No click ID, no postback. No postback, no learning.
d.s: This lesson connects the network's money events to Meta.

steps.say: Here's why this matters. Registrations and deposits happen on the advertiser's site. The only way you, and Meta, learn about them is the network's postback. Without it, Meta optimises on clicks and leads, while your profit is decided somewhere it can't see. Remember the line on screen: no click I D, no postback. No postback, no learning.

steps.p: Follow one person. Your lander creates a click ID and saves the click's details. The offer link carries that ID in sub1. When the person deposits, the network calls your postback URL with sub1 filled in. Your server finds the saved click and sends Purchase to Meta.
steps.say: Let's follow one person around this loop. Your lander creates a click I D and saves the click's details, like F B C, I P and user agent. The offer link carries that I D in sub one. The person deposits, and the network records an F T D, a first time deposit. Then the network calls your postback U R L with sub one filled in. Your server looks up the saved click, and sends Purchase to Meta through the Conversions API.

steps.p: Example week on a trading offer paying $45 per FTD. 900 clicks reached the lander, 210 tapped the button (Lead), 40 registered and 7 deposited. One FTD was later rejected, so 6 count. Every row after Lead came from postbacks.

steps.p: Find your symptom in the first column. Do the fix, then retest from the start of the chain. Most problems here are one of these seven.
steps.say: Find your symptom in the first column, then read across to the likely cause and the fix. No PageView: a blocker, or missing code. Two PageViews per load: installed twice. Leads equal visits: Lead fires on load. Server events rejected: a bad token, I D or time. Not deduplicated: the event I D differs. Events only in Test events: the test code is still on. A sudden drop to zero: a revoked token or server down. After any fix, retest from the very start of the chain.

steps.p: These symptoms show up in the network panel, your log or reporting. Always look at the raw postback log first: it tells you whether the problem is before or after your server.

The macro text showing in your log: wrong macro. Postbacks for unknown clicks: sub one is empty, or clicks were deleted. No postback at all: wrong U R L or event. An absurd purchase value: mixed currencies. Results doubled after adding the Conversions API: no deduplication. And Meta far below the network: weak matching or late sends.

steps.p: Event Match Quality (EMQ) is Meta's score, out of 10, for how well an event's customer data can be matched to a Meta account. Better matching usually means better optimisation and attribution. Meta shows it per event in Events Manager.
steps.more: We are not certain how Meta calculates or labels EMQ today; it has changed over time. Use it as a direction: a rising score after you add fbc or hashed email means the change helped. Do not chase a perfect 10 by collecting data you have no reason or consent to collect.

steps.say: Event Match Quality, or E M Q, is Meta's score out of ten for how well an event's customer data can be matched to a Meta account. Better matching usually means better optimisation and attribution. The number on screen, six point two, is the score for the server Purchase in our example. As a rough guide, not an official threshold, above six is workable, and below four means matching data is missing. We're not certain how Meta calculates it today, so use it as a direction. And don't chase a perfect ten by collecting data you have no reason or consent to collect.

steps.p: Matching improves with more, fresher and correctly formatted identifiers. Add them roughly in this order, and only within what your privacy notice says and your visitors agreed to.
d: fbc|From fbclid; the strongest link to an ad click
fbp|The pixel's browser ID from the _fbp cookie
IP and user agent|From the visitor's original request, not your server's
Hashed email or phone|Only when collected with consent
external_id|Your hashed click or user ID, same on browser and server
steps.say: So what raises match quality? More, fresher and correctly formatted identifiers. Add them roughly in this order. F B C, from the click I D, the strongest link to an ad click. F B P, the pixel's browser I D. The visitor's I P address and user agent, from their original request, not your server's. Hashed email or phone, only when collected with consent. And external I D, your hashed click or user I D, the same on browser and server. Always stay within what your privacy notice says and your visitors agreed to.

steps.p: Example: Meta shows 15 of 20 approved FTDs, 75%. Log check: 1 postback had empty sub1 from an old ad link. 2 were sent days late by a batch job and rejected as too old. 2 were not attributed to an ad. Fix the link and send in real time.
steps.more: Attribution gaps are normal. Someone may click your ad, then deposit after the attribution window, or on a device Meta cannot connect. Fix what is in your control (IDs, speed, matching data) and accept a residual gap. Rough guide, varies by geo and vertical: many operators see Meta report somewhere around 70 to 90% of network conversions once tracking is clean.

steps.p: These are starting rules to adapt to your own offers. They stop you scaling on broken data, and they stop you killing a good campaign because of a tracking fault rather than a bad ad.

rows: Meta < 70% of approved FTDs for 3 days
Results jump > 30% after a tracking change
Server errors > 5% of sends in a day
Fix before launching new ad sets
0 events in 24 h, spend ≥ 1 × target CPA
Gap stable 75 to 90% for a week

steps.say: These are starting rules to adapt to your own offers. They stop you scaling on broken data, and they stop you killing a good campaign because of a tracking fault. Read each one. Meta under seventy percent of approved F T Ds for three days: freeze budget and audit the chain. Results jump over thirty percent after a tracking change: check deduplication before scaling. Server errors above five percent in a day: fix before new ad sets. Zero events in twenty four hours with spend of one times your target C P A, cost per acquisition: pause and rerun the test. And a stable gap of seventy five to ninety percent: normal, judge profit on the network.

steps.p: Clean tracking is also lawful tracking. Your privacy notice must say what you collect, why, who you share it with (Meta, your network) and how long you keep it. Where the law requires consent, honour refusals in the browser and on the server.

d.text: Laws to check include Nigeria's NDPA 2023, Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019, South Africa's POPIA and Ghana's Data Protection Act 2012. Rules change and other geos differ; check the regulator's site and get local advice.

lessons.title: Telegram join tracking setup
objectives: By the end you can explain why the pixel cannot see Telegram joins and what replaces it
By the end you can choose between one join link per ad set and one per click
By the end you can set up a bot that approves join requests and records which link was used
By the end you can send a join to Meta as a server event tied to the original ad click

steps.h: The pixel cannot follow anyone into Telegram
steps.p: Why it matters: in a Telegram funnel, the moment that counts is the join, and it happens inside the Telegram app. No pixel runs there. Without join tracking, Meta only sees taps on your lander and keeps buying people who tap but never join.

d.b: The join is a server event
d.s: Your bot sees it, your server tells Meta.

steps.say: Here's why this matters. In a Telegram funnel, the moment that counts is the join, and it happens inside the Telegram app, where no pixel runs. Without join tracking, Meta only sees taps on your lander, and keeps buying people who tap but never join. So, as the slide says, the join is a server event. Your bot sees it, and your server tells Meta.

steps.p: One join-request link per ad set is simple and gives clean counts per source. One link per click ties each join to one ad click, which is what Meta needs to optimise. Start with per ad set links to count, and add per-click links when you want Meta to learn from joins.

a.title: One link per ad set
items: Create links by hand in the app
Counts joins per source
Cannot tell Meta which click joined
Good for reporting only

b.title: One link per click
items: Bot creates a link for each visitor
Each join maps to one saved click
Join sent to Meta with fbc, fbp, IP, UA
Good for reporting and optimisation

steps.say: There are two ways to track joins. Compare the columns. On the left, one join request link per ad set. You create the links by hand, and you get clean counts per source, but you can't tell Meta which click joined. It's good for reporting only. On the right, one link per click. Your bot creates a link for each visitor, each join maps to one saved click, and the join goes to Meta with the matching data. That's good for reporting and optimisation. Start with per ad set links to count, and add per click links when you want Meta to learn from joins.

steps.p: The lander saves the click as in lesson 5. When the visitor taps Join, your server asks the bot to create an invite link named with the click ID. The person sends a join request. Telegram tells your bot which link was used, the bot approves, and your server sends the join to Meta.
steps.say: This map shows the per click flow. Follow it from the ad. The lander saves the click, just like the last lesson. When the visitor taps Join, your server asks the bot to create an invite link named with the click I D. The visitor opens Telegram and sends a join request. Telegram tells your bot which link was used. The bot approves, and your server sends the join to Meta through the Conversions API.

steps.say: You need a bot that's an admin of your channel, with the right to invite users. Let's walk through it. First, open the official BotFather chat, send the new bot command, and give it a name and a username ending in bot. Second, BotFather replies with a token; store it as a server secret, just like your Meta token. Third, in your channel, add the bot as an administrator and switch on Invite users via link, leaving other rights off. Finally, point the bot at your server with a webhook, including a secret token so only Telegram can call it. Telegram's menus change between versions.

steps.h: Create one invite link per click
steps.p: When the visitor taps Join, your server calls createChatInviteLink. The name holds the click ID (names can be up to 32 characters). creates_join_request makes it a request link. An expiry date stops old links being shared around.
steps.more: We are not certain how many invite links a channel can hold or how fast a bot may create them; Telegram does not publish all limits and they can change. At higher volume, create links in advance in small batches, reuse expired ones carefully, or fall back to per ad set links if you hit errors. Respect any Too Many Requests error and its retry time.

d.text:
curl -X POST "https://api.telegram.org/bot<BOT_TOKEN>/createChatInviteLink" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "chat_id": -1001234567890,
    "name": "c_8f3a9c21",
    "creates_join_request": true,
    "expire_date": <UNIX_TIME_PLUS_1_DAY>
  }'

# Reply (shortened):
# {"ok":true,"result":{"invite_link":"https://t.me/+AbCdEf123...",
#   "name":"c_8f3a9c21","creates_join_request":true, ...}}
d.note: Your server then redirects the visitor to the returned t.me/+ link.

steps.say: When the visitor taps Join, your server asks Telegram to create an invite link. Look at the request on screen; you don't need to read it. Three settings matter. The name holds the click I D, up to thirty two characters. The join request setting makes it a request link. And an expiry date stops old links being shared around. Your server then redirects the visitor to the link Telegram returns. We're not certain how many links a channel can hold or how fast a bot can make them, so if you hit errors, slow down or fall back to per ad set links.

steps.p: When someone taps Request to Join, Telegram sends a chat_join_request update. The part you need is invite_link.name, which is your click ID. Links created by the bot itself come through in full; links made by other admins may arrive shortened, so let the bot create them.

steps.h: Worked example: cost per join and per member
steps.p: Example: $90 spend. 1,000 lander visits, 380 taps on Join, 250 join requests, all approved. After 7 days, 160 are still members. Cost per join: 90 ÷ 250 = $0.36. Cost per retained member: 90 ÷ 160 ≈ $0.56. Tap to request: 250 ÷ 380 ≈ 66%.
steps.more: Joins are not money. Only FTDs from the offer pay you. Track both: cost per retained member tells you about the audience; cost per FTD (from postbacks via your click IDs in the channel's offer links) tells you about profit. If you post offer links inside the channel, give each post its own sub2 so you can see which post produces deposits.

d.text: Starting rules to adapt: if under 50% of taps become join requests, fix the join page and message match first. If cost per retained member is over 2× your target after spend ≥ 2× target, kill that ad set.

Starting rules to adapt: if under fifty percent of taps become requests, fix the join page first. If cost per retained member is over two times your target after spending two times target, kill that ad set. And remember, joins aren't money. Only F T Ds pay you.

lessons.say_intro: In this lesson you'll set up Telegram join tracking. The join happens inside Telegram, where no pixel can run, so you'll use a bot and your server to tell Meta who joined and from which click.
lessons.say_outro: You can now explain why the pixel can't see joins, choose between per ad set and per click links, set up a bot that approves requests, and send a join to Meta tied to the original click. Your task: make your bot an admin of a test channel, set its webhook with a secret token, create one invite link named with a test click I D, request to join from your phone and confirm the join appears with that name in your server log. Now take the quiz.

exam.q: You launch on Monday. By Wednesday the network shows 4 approved FTDs at $40 but Meta shows 0 Purchases. Test events show PageView and Lead fine. Where do you look first?
options: Your postback log: did postbacks arrive, and did sub1 match a saved click?
exam.why: Browser events work, so the break is after the offer: postback delivery, macros or click matching.

exam.q: Budget $25 a day. Cost per registration about $5, cost per FTD about $30. Which optimisation event is the most sensible start?
options: Purchase, because it is worth the most
CompleteRegistration (about 35 a week), while still sending Purchase
exam.why: 25 ÷ 5 = 5 a day, 35 a week, versus under 6 FTDs a week; start where Meta gets enough signal.

exam.q: After adding server Leads, Ads Manager shows 140 Leads for $210, up from 85. Test events show browser and server Leads but none marked deduplicated. What is the true cost per lead likely closer to?
options: About $2.47 or higher, because many of the 140 are duplicates
exam.why: Without matching event_ids, copies are double counted; 210 ÷ 85 ≈ $2.47 is closer to reality until deduplication works.

exam.q: A teammate pasted your Conversions API token into the lander's JavaScript to save time. What do you do?
options: Leave it, the pixel ID is public anyway
Remove it, generate a new token, revoke the old one and keep the new one in server secrets
exam.why: A token in page code is public; anyone can poison your pixel, so rotate it and keep it server-side.

exam.q: Your postback log shows 12 calls with cid=c_... values but 9 say 'unknown click'. The lander and offer link were changed last week. Most likely cause?
options: The new link stopped passing your click ID correctly, or click records are not being saved
exam.why: Unknown clicks mean the ID in the postback does not match a saved click; check the new link and the /api/click save.

exam.q: Network: 25 approved FTDs this week. Meta: 23 Purchases, 2 of which the network later rejected. Spend $800, payout $40. What is your real profit?
exam.why: 25 approved × $40 = $1,000 revenue; 1,000 − 800 = $200. Judge money on approved network numbers.

exam.q: You set up Telegram per-click links, but join updates arrive with no usable link name. The links were made by your assistant in the Telegram app. Fix?
options: Have the bot create the links through createChatInviteLink
exam.why: The bot needs to read the link name; links it creates itself arrive in full.

exam.q: Meta shows 62% of approved network FTDs for 4 days running. Your starting rules say?
options: Freeze budget and audit the chain station by station
exam.why: Below about 70% for 3+ days means something is likely broken; stop adding budget and find the leak.

exam.q: A visitor declined tracking in your consent banner, so the pixel did not load. Your server still has their click data. What should happen?
options: Send everything by CAPI, since the browser missed it
Respect the refusal: do not send their events to Meta by CAPI
Send it hashed so it does not count
exam.why: Consent applies to server events too; hashing does not make refused tracking lawful.

exam.q: You want to test the full FTD path on a live trading offer before launch. Which is right?
options: Ask the affiliate manager to fire a test FTD postback for your test click ID, with your test event code on
Make a small real deposit using a friend's identity
Send a Purchase to Meta by hand from curl with no test code
exam.why: A network test conversion checks the same path without breaking offer terms or polluting live data.
